output.summary:
The document describes the Address Resolution (AR) protocol, designed to allow machines on an Ethernet network to dynamically discover and maintain mappings between higher-level network protocols (e.g., Internet, CHAOS) and physical 48-bit Ethernet hardware addresses. It details the structure of AR packets—including request/reply types and various address fields—and explains how the protocol functions: when a machine needs to send data to a destination IP address but doesn't know the corresponding MAC address, it broadcasts an AR REQUEST. Upon receiving this, the target machine replies with an AR REPLY containing its hardware address, which is then used by the originating machine to correctly forward the original data packet.

The document also addresses advanced, non-critical topics like table aging and timeouts, suggesting mechanisms such as using periodic keep-alive requests or relying on network events (like a host reboot) to prevent stale mappings from causing communication failures.

key_concepts.description: A mechanism allowing machines on an Ethernet cable to dynamically discover the physical MAC address associated with a known higher-level protocol and IP address. It is necessary because upper-layer protocols (like IP) use logical addresses, while the local link layer (Ethernet) requires physical hardware addresses.

The packet contains specific fields: target/sender Ethernet and protocol addresses, a request/reply opcode (ar$op), and length indicators (ar$hln, ar$pln). The presence of the target protocol address in the request form is crucial for determining if the sender should record information or send a reply.

A machine needing an address sends a broadcast AR REQUEST. The intended recipient, upon recognizing its own IP address and protocol type in the packet, replies directly to the source with an AR REPLY containing its hardware MAC address. This reply allows the original sender to complete the necessary mapping.

The protocol is valuable for network monitoring because a passive monitor can analyze broadcasted AR packets to determine which higher-level protocols are active and what address mappings are being established, without needing to understand the specifics of those upper-layer protocols.

While outside the scope of the core protocol, best practices suggest implementing mechanisms (like periodic keep-alive requests or monitoring packet receipt) to delete stale address mappings from the translation table, preventing communication failures when a host's IP assignment changes.
